https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/03/guar.text: Menü Kereső A Guardian arról ír, a magyarok Hide the Pain Haroldot és Palvin Barbarát is szívesen látnák az elnöki székben Belföld Aradi Hanga Zsófia Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Messzire ér a megüresedett köztársasági elnöki szék sorsának kérdése. A brit Guardian hétfőn arról írt , miután Magyar Péter miniszterelnök arra szólította fel a magyarokat, ajánljanak neveket a posztra, hogy a reális javaslatok mellett egészen abszurd, de annál népszerűbb jelöltek is szóba kerültek a közösségi médiában. Ilyen például a nyugdíjas villamosmérnök, Arató András, ismertebb nevén Hide the Pain Harold, aki a lap szerint egy online felmérés alapján a legnépszerűbb jelölt. Előkelő helyen végzett Karikó Katalin Nobel-díjas kutató és Rubik Ernő, a Rubik-kocka alkotója is. Egy másik, Jámbor Eszter influenszer által indított szavazáson ennél is változatosabb lett a potenciális jelöltek listája, a követői testépítőket, realitysztárokat is ajánlottak a posztra, és felmerült az Egyesült Államokban élő, éppen gyereket váró Palvin Barbara modell neve is. Papíron egyébként a harminckét éves modellt leszámítva bármelyikük esélyes lehet a posztra. Köztársasági elnöknek ugyanis az Alaptörvény szerint bármely magyar állampolgár megválasztható, aki elmúlt harmincöt éves. Hosszas huzavona és ide-oda üzengetés után a Tisza Párt végül az Alaptörvény módosításával érte el, hogy elmozdítsa a helyéről az általuk Fidesz-bábnak nevezett Sulyok Tamást a köztársasági elnöki székből. Sulyok az utolsó pillanatban aláírta az Alaptörvény 17. módosítását , ezzel egy csapásra meg is szűnt a megbízatása. A köztársasági elnöki tisztséget Sulyok Tamás távozásával ideiglenesen Forsthoffer Ágnes, az Országgyűlés elnöke vette át. Ezzel párhuzamosan nagy erőkkel indult el a következő köztársasági elnök castingja, ami rögtön buktával kezdődött, hiába kérte ugyanis Magyar Péter a magyarokat, hogy ajánljanak neveket, alig egy nappal később már arról írt , Polgár Judit megfelelő lenne a posztra, és megtisztelő lenne, ha vállalná. Ezt a Tisza-frakció is megerősítette, de hiába, Polgár ugyanis megköszönte, de visszautasította a felkérést. A Tisza Párt azóta hivatalosan nem javasolt még senkit a pozícióra, de Magyar Péter két potenciális jelölttel is találkozott: Romsics Ignác Széchenyi-díjas történésszel és a Vidéki prókátor néven ismertté vált ügyvéddel, Fülöp Botonddal is. Magyar egyébként korábban azt ígérte, augusztus 20-án már új köztársasági elnöke lesz az országnak. A köztársasági elnök személyéről a parlament dönt, ahhoz, hogy valakinek a neve felkerüljön a szavazólapra, az országgyűlési képviselők legalább egyötöde, azaz 40 képviselő ajánlására van szükség. A Tisza Párt mellett így egyedül a 44 fős Fidesz-frakció tudna önállóan köztársasági elnököt állítani, a KDNP vagy a Mi Hazánk a Fidesz nélkül nem tudja ezt megtenni. A Fidesz és a KDNP azonban korábban azt jelezte, hogy bojkottálják az államfőválasztást. A Mi Hazánk múlt héten dr. Tóth Máté energiajogászt jelölte a posztra, ami más frakciók támogatása nélkül tulajdonképpen csak szimbolikus gesztus. A köztársaságielnök-castingban nehéz helyzetbe kormányozta magát a Tisza Párt, a Medián szerint ez is hozzájárulhatott enyhe népszerűség-csökkenésükhöz. https://www.gdnonline.com:443/Details/14.text: Police officers and Spanish soldiers escort a group of migrants to the border to take them out of Spain in Ceuta Spain has condemned the ‘selfish, polarising and unlawful’ reaction of some EU countries to the influx of about 60,000 migrants from Morocco into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta. Spanish officials say almost all those who reached Ceuta on July 30 have returned, while Spain’s interior minister said yesterday that the death toll from the surge in crossings had risen to at least 86. Italy temporarily suspended the EU’s border-free Schengen arrangement with Spain, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the scenes ‘shocking’. Finland and Denmark backed Italy’s move, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis urged a temporary suspension of Spain’s Schengen membership. EU interior ministers will meet on Tuesday by video conference to discuss the issue. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had called for an urgent meeting to ‘reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a shared responsibility of all member states’. Twenty-two of the EU’s 27 countries also called for emergency talks in an open letter, citing ‘serious concerns’ regarding the developments in Ceuta. In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Sanchez said he had ‘serious concerns’ about some European governments. He said the Spanish government had fully restored control over the border and prevented any ‘unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe’ in less than 48 hours. While most had shown ‘support and solidarity’, Sanchez said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, ‘driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest’, and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area. “The European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction,” he said. Also yesterday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he had spoken to Sanchez and the UK was ‘providing what help we can’. There were chaotic scenes on Thursday in Ceuta as border controls in the North African enclave apparently broke down. But in a news conference yesterday, Spain’s Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told reporters the situation in Ceuta had almost returned to normal. “Almost all of (the migrants) have already left Ceuta,” the minister said, adding that businesses had now reopened. “The situation has been almost entirely reversed.” He also said Spain had started to establish an inflatable maritime barrier to prevent further illegal migrant entry. But while the situation on the ground appears to be easing, political and diplomatic fallout is rippling through Madrid and other capitals. On Thursday, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on social media that such ‘uncontrolled immigration’ was a threat to national security, before suspending the Schengen zone agreement with Spain for a month. The Schengen Area is a system of open borders spanning 29 European countries that have abolished controls at their common borders. Spain responded by summoning the Italian ambassador to Madrid, while its foreign minister said he expected ‘European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery’. Finland’s Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said she had started preparations for restoring internal border checks ‘if the need arises’. She also urged ‘all European countries’ to support Meloni’s move. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen also urged the EU to ‘consider all options, including a suspension of Schengen co-operation’. France has tightened checks on its border with Spain and said it would increase its police presence.

https://www.bgr.com/2256265/best-filamen.text: Technology Accessories The 5 Best Filaments You Can Buy For 3D Printers By Christian Wait Sept. 20, 2026 11:17 am EST Stenko Vlad/Shutterstock Add BGR on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. No matter who makes an FDM 3D printer or how much it costs, cheap filament isn't going to give users the results they expect. In my experience, investing in a cheaper 3D printer and buying the right filament is a better choice than buying an expensive printer and using questionable filament spools from the odd corners of eBay. Many users, myself included, typically stick to one of two brands because they just work. There's nothing wrong with that of course, but there's so many filaments and brands worth trying that produce different or better results. This goes beyond where you get STL files, which can include open source 3D project models . This is about material. PLA is popular for 3D printings, but there's very cool uses for stronger filaments such as PETG and flexible ones like TPU too. For people willing to step out of their comfort zones, there are all sorts of projects including working grips for a workshop, or shock absorbing phone cases, that they can make with different filaments. Buying from popular 3D printer brands is a good place to start. A spool of filament from industry names like Prusament PLA are a great way to guarantee better results than a $5 roll from a random dropshipper on TikTok. Trust me, I've been there. Below are five filament brands and types I would happily use (and tried) for any of my projects on my Prusa XL 5-head and Elegoo Centauri Carbon. Voxel PLA+ Amazon Starting with the basic PLA filament, Voxel PLA+ is a great choice that can be picked up for $16.99 for a 1-kilogram (2.2 pounds) spool, with 3 kilograms (6.6 pounds) costing $50.97. Buying in bulk is where Voxel's pricing really kicks in, with 6-to-10 1-kilogram spools costing $16.55 apiece, 11-30 at $16.15 each, and 31-50 for $15.98-per-spool. PLA has a low melting point, low thermal expansion, good layer adhesion, minimal warping, and is perfect for anything ornamental and low stress applications. Voxel PLA+ has a print temperature of between 200 degreess Celsius and 220 degrees Celsius (392 degrees Fahrenheit to 428 degrees Fahrenheit). Its bed temperature is up to 60 degrees Celsius (140 degrees Fahrenheit), The spools come vacuum-packed in 21 basic colors. For bulk buyers, these colors can be a mix of whatever suits their needs. All of Voxels filaments are engineered and made in Southern California, where the company also operates a farm of 250 3D printers. There's nothing like a company putting its money where its mouth is in my opinion, and each spool is a plastic one, meaning it'll work in any automatic AMS multicolor setups. Don't try using a cardboard spool, it didn't end well for me. Overall Voxel PLA+ prints really nicely and keep up with my favorite brand, Prusament, in terms of quality and adhesion. Assuming you stick to the slower print speeds and the right supports, there's very little post processing to do whenever I've used this filament. Prusament Prusa Prusament is the gold standard for me and is often seen as a premium option. Coming in at $26.99 per 1-kilogram for PLA, the consistency in this brand is excellent. The company even includes a QR code on every spool that logs how and when each of them was made. The quality control is also excellent, with Prusa saying that every batch tested against the standard colorway before shipping. This is a godsend for massive prints, like when I printed out a white two-tone Stormtrooper helmet by using two cheap rolls of filament when starting out. Prusa says it holds a strict diameter tolerance limit of ±0.04 millimeters, and publishes information about that on its website. One of my pet peeves with cheap spools is they sometimes include tangled filament that can halt a long overnight project. Prusa says its spools are wound on machines that use controlled tension to ensure consistency. It's nice to see a manufacturer putting so much care into things like this that are often overlooked. Best of all, Prusa spools are now also made in Delaware as well as the Czech Republic, so makers don't need to worry about import duties and long shipping times. Every kind of Prusa filament I've tried, including PLA, PETG, and glow-in-the-dark, have all run perfectly on both of my 3D printers. I'd sooner spend a little bit more and save on print failure headaches. PolyLite PETG from Polymaker Amazon PETG is best described as "taking off the training wheels" when stepping up from PLA, in my experience. PETG is stronger and has better heat and sunlight resistance, with more flexibility than PLA. That combination makes it perfect for practical use for outdoor objects like bird feeders to tire air caps. But it's also harder to print due to higher temperatures needed, among other things. I found Polymaker's PolyLite PETG to be a good budget option at $15.99 for a 1-kilogram spool. It has a heat resistance of up to 80 degrees Celsius (176 degrees Fahrenheit), so it's great material for printing out casings and shrouds for electronics like a Raspberry Pi build. It's tangle free and comes delivered vacuum packed to avoid moisture, which is great when storing bulk filament. Higher temperatures create more wear and tear on the 3D printer, so before committing to printing in PETG, make sure to check over instruction booklets on what your 3D printer can handle. Budget 3D printers don't typically work with PETG filament unless specifically stated, because of temperature constraints. Also, even if your printer can handle PETG, it's good to swap out any standard brass nozzles with hardened steel to help too. Polymaker's take on PETG wasn't an issue for me, I just made sure to turn my printer head fans off in-slicer for the first layer so it adheres properly. Inland TPU Micro Center I love making things with TPU. Tt bends without breaking and has a rubber feel, making it great for practical projects like door handles, phone cases, and seals. Overall toughness is determined by the amount of infill given in-slicer, with around 50% being enough for a tough yet flexible build when I've used it, just use less for more flexibility. The biggest point to make when working with TPU like the one Inland produces is that you should use a direct drive print head. This means the motor and gears that push filament into the extruder need to be positioned directly on top of the print head due to how flexible TPU is. If you're not using direct drive, it's not worth just trying and hoping for the best. In my experience, it fails otherwise. Inland TPU is currently $21.99 at Micro Center for a 1-kilogram spool. It needs between 210 and 240 degrees Celsius print temperature to flow properly with a bed temperature between 60 degrees Celsius (140 degrees Fahrenheit) and 80 degrees Celsius (176 degrees Fahrenheit) for proper adhesion. For anything that needs to absorb impact, grip, or flex, TPU is the best filament for the job, with Inland being readily available for delivery from Micro Center. Protopasta Recycled PLA Amazon For makers looking for a cheeky bargain while getting the same quality as the premium alternative, Protopasta Recycled PLA is a great choice. The company collects its own waste stream from filament production to make the recycled PLA that's fully compounded for the same performance when printing. It may contain sparkles of different color dependent on the waste stream used for a particular batch, that works well when trying STL files from obscure 3D printing sites . It's also cheaper. Protopasta charges $19.99 for its 1-kilogram spool, a $10 saving when compared to its standard black PLA spool at $29.99 on Amazon. That's great for makers like myself who print off in any color, then prime and paint whatever colors they need. Both the recycled and standard PLA spools are made in the U.S. and are standardized to a 1.75 millimeter diameter alongside making sure it has less embedded moisture to flow better than other standard PLA filaments. This helps avoid excess heat absorption, and forms better on build plates. As previously mentioned, I love a tangle-free spool, and Protopasta's recycled filament is just that, albeit on a one-use cardboard spool. Make sure to avoid putting this in any automatic filament dispensers unless it's on a filament hook like on the side of the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 or Prusa XL. Recommended

Photograph: Rhett Hammerton/EPA View image in fullscreen The Warlpiri girl was allegedly abducted and murdered in Alice Springs in April. Photograph: Rhett Hammerton/EPA Indigenous Australians Kumanjayi Little Baby: damning report finds ‘heartbreaking’ child protection failures before five-year-old’s death Northern Territory government announced sweeping reforms of child protection sector in May, just days after the Warlpiri girl was found dead Warning: This article contains images of and references to Indigenous Australians who have died Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Douglas Smith Indigenous affairs reporter Mon 19 Oct 2026 21.50 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 21.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A report into the Northern Territory’s child protection sector has detailed “confronting” and “heartbreaking” failures in the lead-up to the alleged murder of Warlpiri girl Kumanjayi Little Baby. The five-year-old was found dead in April, five days after she was allegedly abducted from a town camp in Alice Springs . Police then charged Jefferson Lewis, a 47-year-old man who was not a member of the child’s family or known to her mother, with murder. He has been remanded in custody and is yet to ender a plea. The minister for children and families, Robyn Cahill, tabled the report in NT parliament on Tuesday. The NT government commissioned the independent review, conducted by former New South Wales police commissioner, Karen Webb, and senior public servant Greg Shanahan, in the wake of the child’s death. Cahill said the report showed a “recurrent pattern” of how police worked alongside the department, which allowed children to be placed in the care of adults without a criminal background check. “[There were] serious gaps between what the law required of the department, and how the law was applied,” she told parliament. “Gaps in policy, in process, and most critically, gaps in how risk to children was being assessed. “Kumanjayi Little Baby’s family was known to the department before she was born. Her mother was assaulted at least twice while she was pregnant with her. When she was 17 weeks old, a safety plan was put in place that relied on adults from the family’s network to keep her safe. The review found no evidence that police or background checks were done on any of them. “It was later established that one of those adults had a long and violent criminal history. Including five counts of threat-to-kill. “These were the adults trusted to keep a baby safe. How can something as basic as checking if they are safe to be around children not be standard practice.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Cahill said the NT government accepted all 45 recommendations made by the report. The interim report, released in July , said “the review team have not been able to draw a nexus between the matters referred to DCF [the Department of Children and Families] and the circumstances leading to KLB’s [Kumanjayi Little Baby’s] abduction”. It said the child’s mother had been the victim of domestic and family violence, but that: “Despite repeated indicators of domestic and family violence, the cumulative impact of the violence and its implications for the child’s safety were not adequately recognised, and protective responses were not pursued in a timely manner.” Explore more on these topics Indigenous Australians Northern Territory Australian police and policing Child protection Alice Springs Northern Territory politics Domestic violence news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story The guard promised to protect Aaron. News and Current Affairs Newsflash Today in the News Sport The Week in Review Features and Reports The History Show Inside Romania Society Today Traveller’s Guide The Future Starts Today Green Planet World of Culture RRI Encyclopaedia Close-Up Romania. The Eastern Flank Working in Romania New Names on the Cover The Cooking Show Expat in Romania RRI Special The Sounds of Romania Voices from the Archives Our Shows Listeners’ Corner Romanian without Tears Sunday Show In the Spotlight Through the Looking Glass Change Makers Happening in Romania Music Time Artscape Weekend Edition On demand LISTEN HERE Useful information Things to know How to listen Forum QSL QSL-cards Homepage » Panoramice » RRI Encyclopaedia » The Institute of Forensic Medicine, or Bucharest’s lost heritage The Institute of Forensic Medicine, or Bucharest’s lost heritage After 93 years of existence, the imposing building was razed as part of the brutal urban redevelopment plan for Bucharest decided by Nicolae Ceaușescu following the earthquake of 4 March 1977. Sergiu Celibidache (1912-1996) Steliu Lambru , 18.10.2026, 14:00 On the left bank of the Dâmbovița, after the river leaves the central area around Unirii Square, stood until 1985 the building of the Institute of Forensic Medicine, named after its founder, Dr Mina Minovici. It was a magnificent building, remarkable both for its architecture and for its purpose. It had been built in the second half of the 19th century, during a period of economic growth in Romania, under King Carol I, with this very purpose in mind. Inaugurated in 1892 as the City Morgue, it became the Institute of Forensic Medicine in 1898. After 93 years of existence, the imposing building was razed as part of the brutal urban redevelopment plan for Bucharest decided by Nicolae Ceaușescu following the earthquake of 4 March 1977. Thus, the Institute of Forensic Medicine became one of the many victims of the inexplicable demolitions of that period. Octavian Buda is a professor of the history of medicine at the Carol Davila University of Medicine and Pharmacy in Bucharest and a psychiatrist at the Mina Minovici Institute of Forensic Medicine. His experience of that building dates back to his youth, when he was preparing to study medicine and was deprived of the heritage left by previous generations: “One rather depressing record we hold in urban history is that we have a morgue that has literally died, namely through the demolition of this building, which had truly remarkable architectural value. This happened around 1985, when I was preparing to sit the entrance examination for medical school. I happened to find myself in the Căuzași area, and as I walked around there, I had the distinct feeling that the whole situation was more than depressing. It is very difficult to put into words why a building was demolished when, in terms of its location, it was practically behind what is now the National Library.” Like St Vineri Church, Văcărești Monastery and other buildings of great architectural value, the Institute of Forensic Medicine was also needlessly demolished. Octavian Buda: “The reason why the building was demolished was utterly incomprehensible, because it was not bothering anyone. According to popular lore, Ceaușescu is supposed to have said: ‘What is this, medicine for the dead? There is no such thing. If it is a morgue for collecting corpses, then it should be moved to the outskirts of the city!’ Interestingly enough, the autopsy and photographing of the man who was shot [Ceaușescu himself] ultimately became an unmistakable document in forensic medicine and the history of forensic medicine. So, in the end, he did not escape what he had tried to avoid.” The Bucharest institute’s building had been modelled on similar institutions in the West, with the Liverpool institution dating from 1837 being its closest source of inspiration, as Octavian Buda has also pointed out. Octavian Buda: “The whole area there, both behind the National Library and opposite it, has remained an empty plot of land where Ceaușescu wanted to build some sort of congress centre. So the demolition took place sometime around 1985. One thing that made a particularly strong impression on me was visiting Liverpool. The city has a building called the Liverpool Medical Institute, which looks remarkably similar to the former Institute of Forensic Medicine in Bucharest. It has much the same structure, with a very large and beautiful entrance hall and an amphitheatre. It has a few more columns than our old morgue. The resemblance is unmistakable: the colonnades, the entrance used by the director and as the main access to the building, and then the interior beyond it.” The beautiful lost building had all the necessary facilities. Octavian Buda: “What is truly remarkable is that such a beautiful and distinctive building could be created and inaugurated on the banks of the Dâmbovița. The institute had certain features that set it apart. It was not merely a morgue where bodies were stored and autopsies performed. It had departments and laboratories for toxicology, anthropometry and identification, which gave these activities a high degree of specialisation. Initially, it was called the City Morgue, after which its name was changed to the Institute of Forensic Medicine. At the entrance to the institute was a room leading to the director’s office. Inside, there was the main autopsy room, with an upper gallery where students would sit all around and look down at the autopsy taking place below. There was another autopsy room, added later, areas where bodies were stored, a room for practical classes for students, the toxicology laboratory, the library and a museum containing all sorts of gruesome exhibits. The museum was open to visitors and was a kind of, as we might call it today, cabinet of curiosities, with all sorts of exhibits and extraordinary specimens. There was also a chapel, built in a beautiful neo-Gothic style, as well as the institute’s small and large amphitheaters.” However, the history of the Institute of Forensic Medicine continued. After operating temporarily at the 23 August Hospital for several years, it moved in 1989 to a building in the style of totalitarian architecture, located on the south-eastern outskirts of the city.
